html:
Potosí, in the high Andes of what is now Bolivia, sits below the Cerro Rico, the "rich mountain". From its discovery in 1545 it was the greatest silver mine in the world for a century, and its silver changed the world economy.

Tradition credits an Indigenous prospector, Diego Huallpa, with the find. A mining town grew almost overnight at about 4,000 metres. By about 1600 it may have held around 150,000 people, as many as the largest cities of Europe, and it ran its own mint.

The work fell on Indigenous people. In the 1570s the viceroy Francisco de Toledo revived the Inca labour draft, the mit'a, and forced thousands of men from across the Andes to serve turns in the mines. Many died from accidents, cold and mercury poisoning; mercury was used to separate silver from ore. "Vale un Potosí", "worth a Potosí", became a Spanish saying for great wealth, while for many Andean families the name meant death.

The silver went in two directions. Some went by llama and mule to the Pacific, then by sea and over the isthmus of Panama to the Spanish treasure fleets and on to Seville. Much of it ended up in China, which wanted silver to pay taxes under the Ming, carried either through Europe and India or across the Pacific on the Manila galleons. Spanish silver coins became the first global currency. Mexico's mines overtook Potosí in the 1700s.
sum: Potosí, in the high Andes of what is now Bolivia, sits below the Cerro Rico, the "rich mountain". From its discovery in 1545 it was the greatest silver mine in the world for a century, and its silver changed the world economy.
